Pascal's Triangle

CountingSequences
Game: Every dot in a triangle of dots has a number: how many ways there are to walk to it from the top dot.
How to play: Press any dot to see the two dots it is reached from, and add their numbers. Change the shape or the number of rows.

Look for the math

Walk down from the top dot, stepping left or right at every dot. The number at a dot is the number of different walks that end there. The numbers are the entries of Pascal's triangle, and they turn out to be the binomial coefficients.

Adding the two dots above

A dot that is not at the end of a row can only be reached from the two dots just above it, and each walk to one of them continues in exactly one way. So C(n, m) = C(n-1, m-1) + C(n-1, m), with C(n, 0) = C(n, n) = 1. Press a dot to see the sum. The test built the triangle this way up to 16 rows.

Counting by choosing

A walk of n steps ending at dot m has m steps to the right and n - m to the left, so the walks are the ways to choose which m of the n steps go right: n choose m. The test also counted every walk of up to 16 steps one by one and got the same rows. The rule above is Pascal's identity.

Two checks to try

Row n adds up to 2n, because there are 2n walks of n steps and each ends somewhere. Every row reads the same backwards, since C(n, m) = C(n, n-m). The test confirmed both for all 16 rows.

Choose "Pascal's" and look along the diagonals. Why do the numbers on a diagonal add up to a number in the next row?
